data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is dominated by stored sensible heat: urban masonry and asphalt absorb daytime solar radiation and, having high thermal mass and heat capacity, release it slowly after sunset, keeping the city warmer than the countryside at night.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rural areas have equivalent or greater thermal mass (e.g., exposed rock), the UHI gap shrinks.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If anthropogenic heat release completely dominates the nocturnal energy balance, thermal mass becomes a secondary effect.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If high wind speeds flush the urban canopy, stored heat is dispersed too rapidly to maintain a temperature gap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, high thermal mass materials in the urban canopy absorb solar radiation. After sunset, the rural countryside cools rapidly, while urban materials release stored sensible heat slowly, sustaining higher temperatures.
